neighbours.label: existentialist philosophy: its thinkers (Sartre, Camus, Kierkegaard, Heidegger, de Beauvoir) and its ideas (existence before essence, freedom and dread, being thrown into the world); nihilism, Stoicism and the everyday word 'existential' stay low
fire: Sartre wrote that man is nothing but what he makes of himself.
In The Stranger, Camus's hero shrugs at his own trial.
Kierkegaard described anxiety as the dizziness of freedom.
Simone de Beauvoir wrote that one is not born a woman but becomes one.
Existentialists insisted that we choose our values rather than find them.
Heidegger asked what it means for a being to exist at all.
The Parisian cafes of the 1940s were full of existentialist writers.
Dostoevsky's underground man is often read as an early existentialist.
quiet: Seneca wrote that we suffer more in imagination than in reality.
In Pride and Prejudice, Austen's heroine laughs at her suitor.
Kant described duty as the necessity of acting from respect for law.
Mary Wollstonecraft wrote that girls should be educated like boys.
Utilitarians insisted that we judge acts by their consequences.
Aristotle asked what it means for a thing to change at all.
The Parisian cafes of the 1920s were full of American writers.
Dickens's Scrooge is often read as a portrait of greed.
